vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits in the therapy office with his shoulders curved inward, his calloused hands—stained with flecks of acrylic and latex paint—folded tightly in his lap. He's twenty-four, lean and quiet, with dark eyes that seem to track movement in the room with heightened awareness. He's been painting professionally for three years now, specializing in interior design work for upscale homes and commercial spaces. It's work he loves, or at least, it's work he used to love.

The relationship with David began eighteen months ago. Marcus had been excited in a way he hadn't felt before—David was charming, attentive, and seemed genuinely interested in Marcus's art. For the first six months, everything felt right. Then, gradually, things shifted. David's comments became sharper. He'd criticize Marcus's work, his appearance, his time spent painting. Marcus remembers thinking it was just passion, just intensity. He made excuses.

Four months ago, after Marcus came home late from a job site, David was waiting. Marcus had missed a call while working on a ceiling detail. What started as an argument escalated quickly. David's hands became fists. Marcus remembers the shock more than the pain at first—the disbelief that this was happening, that David was doing this. He was thrown against the kitchen counter. His left arm bent at an angle that made him cry out. When it was over, David apologized profusely, blamed stress, blamed Marcus for making him angry. Marcus believed him. He told himself it wouldn't happen again.

But it did. Three more times in the following weeks, each incident preceded by a buildup of tension that Marcus learned to dread. He left David six weeks ago, moving back in with his parents in their Southeast Asian community. His mother doesn't ask many questions, but he sees the worry in her face.

Now, Marcus struggles to function in ways he didn't anticipate. His body feels like it's constantly braced for impact. At work, he finds himself jumping at unexpected sounds—when a client enters a room he didn't hear approaching, when a coworker touches his shoulder to get his attention. Last week, a contractor raised his voice during a meeting about measurements, and Marcus felt his chest tighten so severely he had to excuse himself to the bathroom. He sat in a locked stall for twenty minutes, breathing carefully, trying to convince himself he was safe.

The painting itself has become difficult. His hands shake sometimes, especially when he's working in enclosed spaces or when his back is to a doorway. He's turned down three jobs in the past month—work he desperately needs financially. His supervisor has noticed. Marcus has been vague about why, embarrassed to explain. The shame is almost as overwhelming as the fear. In his community, there's an unspoken expectation about how men should handle relationships, about strength and resilience. He feels like he's failed on both counts.

His girlfriend, Sarah, has been patient, but he can sense her frustration. He's withdrawn from her, flinching sometimes when she touches him unexpectedly, even though he knows she means no harm. He wants to be close to her, wants to feel normal again, but his body won't cooperate. Sleep comes fitfully, interrupted by dreams where he's trapped or unable to move. He wakes with his heart racing, disoriented about where he is.

Marcus wants to work again, wants to reclaim the parts of himself that David took. But right now, he exists in a strange liminal space—safe from immediate danger, yet still haunted by the memory of hands that hurt him, still waiting for the next blow that might come.
